title: NMP-PaK: Near-Memory Processing Acceleration of Scalable De Novo Genome Assembly
problem: De novo genome assembly using De Bruijn graph (DBG) algorithms is both memory-latency-bound and memory-footprint-intensive: processing 10% of the human genome (38.3 GB input) requires 528 GB of DRAM, and the Iterative Compaction step—which dominates 48% of runtime—achieves only 2.5% of available memory bandwidth due to fine-grained, irregular access patterns across large, dynamic MacroNode data structures.
method: NMP-PaK places pipelined systolic Processing Elements (PEs) inside DIMM buffer chips (channel-level NMP) to exploit high internal memory bandwidth and reduce data movement latency. Each PE implements a 3-stage pipeline (Invalidation Check, TransferNode Extraction, Routing and Update) operating at MacroNode granularity, with an intra-DIMM crossbar switch and an inter-DIMM network bridge routing TransferNodes between PEs. Software optimizations complement the hardware: customized batch processing divides the genome into 10% batches to reduce peak memory footprint by 14x, pointer-aliasing deduplication eliminates redundant MacroNode copies, and a hybrid CPU-NMP strategy offloads large MacroNodes (>1 KB) to the CPU to avoid PE buffer oversizing and workload imbalance.

title: The Hidden Bloat in Machine Learning Systems
problem: ML frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, MXNet) ship highly bloated shared libraries with large amounts of unused GPU and CPU code, wasting memory, increasing load times, and degrading performance.
method: Negativa-ML hooks the CUDA cuModuleGetFunction API to detect which GPU kernel functions are actually called at runtime per workload. GPU code is localized at the cubin (binary) and element (function) granularity. CPU code analysis uses existing call-graph techniques. Unused GPU cubins and functions are removed from the shared libraries. Evaluated across 4 ML frameworks, 10 workloads, and 300+ shared libraries.

title: Dynamic Input Pruning for Efficient LLM Inference on Mobile Devices
problem: SwiGLU-based LLM MLP layers on mobile devices are memory-bandwidth bound, with all weight matrices (up, gate, down projections) fully loaded from DRAM for every token, causing excessive energy consumption and low throughput.
method: Dynamic Input Pruning (DIP) applies predictor-free top-K selection on MLP input activation magnitudes, selecting only the K largest input elements and pruning corresponding columns of the up, gate, and down projection matrices. No separate predictor network is needed. LoRA adapters can be added for fine-tuning recovery. DIP-CA (cache-aware variant) uses a gamma multiplier (gamma=0.2) to bias selection toward cached weight columns, reducing DRAM refetch. Evaluated via simulation of Apple A18 (60 GB/s DRAM, 1 GB/s Flash) on Phi-3-Medium, LLaMA models.

title: AdaParse: An Adaptive Parallel PDF Parsing and Resource Scaling Engine
problem: Building trillion-token scientific text datasets for LLM pre-training requires parsing millions of PDFs, but state-of-the-art high-quality parsers (e.g., Nougat) can only process 1-2 PDFs/second on a 4-A100 node, while lightweight parsers produce poor quality on complex documents.
method: AdaParse implements a hierarchical three-stage classifier pipeline: CLS I (rule-based validity check on PyMuPDF-extracted text features), CLS II (metadata-driven regression predicting if improvement is likely), CLS III (LLM-based multi-class parser selection). Human preferences are collected from 23 domain experts and incorporated via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to fine-tune the SciBERT-based classifier. Parsl orchestrates parallel execution on HPC (Polaris), batching PDFs, warm-starting ML parsers, and distributing tasks across nodes.

title: Venn: Resource Management for Collaborative Learning Jobs
problem: Multiple concurrent collaborative learning (federated learning) jobs compete for ephemeral, heterogeneous edge devices with overlapping eligibility requirements; existing schedulers use random device-to-job matching, causing high scheduling delays and poor job completion time.
method: Venn: a centralized CL resource manager with two algorithms. (1) Intersection Resource Scheduling (IRS): groups jobs by device requirements into Resource-Homogeneous Job Groups. Within each group, sorts jobs by ascending remaining demand (shortest-first). Across groups, greedily allocates intersected resources to the group with the longer queue-to-resource ratio, prioritizing groups with scarce resources. Algorithm runs in O(max(m log m, n^2)) time. (2) Resource-aware tier-based device matching: partitions eligible devices into V tiers by hardware capability; assigns randomly-selected tier to each job. Triggers tier-based matching only when JCT reduction condition holds (1 + c > V + c*g). Fairness extension adjusts demand weights to prevent starvation.
